analysis.one_liner: Caps spending and PAC money in House races and gives tax credits for small donations.
analysis.headline: The House campaign finance bill never left committee: it drew zero cosponsors and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the money rules for House of Representatives elections. Political action committees could have given a House candidate at most $5,000 total, anyone spending $5,000 or more on ads independent of a campaign would have had to report it to election regulators within 24 hours, and residents of a candidate's district could have given at most $3,000. Candidates who voluntarily agreed to a $500,000 spending cap would have earned two rewards: their small in-district donors would get a federal tax credit of up to $200, and TV and radio stations could charge them only 70% of the normal ad rate. Candidates who broke the cap would have faced penalties and had to refund donations.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in House districts. The bill would have shrunk the role of PAC money and big out-of-district donations in House races, forced rapid public disclosure of large independent ad spending, and given small donors a tax credit so that people of modest means could help fund campaigns on more equal footing with wealthy donors. Candidates who accepted the spending cap would have gotten cheaper airtime, stretching small donations further.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total contributions from any multicandidate political committee to a House candidate at $5,000 for a general election and its primary, tightening the existing per-election limits into one aggregate ceiling.

Requires anyone making independent expenditures of $5,000 or more in a House race to report them to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours, and requires the FEC to pass that information to the candidate involved.

Creates a nonrefundable income tax credit of up to $200 ($400 on joint returns) for contributions by residents of the congressional district to House candidates, and bars estates and trusts from claiming it.

Lets House candidates voluntarily agree to limit spending to $500,000 in a contested election; those who sign up pay no more than 70% of the normal broadcast ad rate, and those who break their pledge face graduated penalties of one to three times the excess plus civil fines and must refund excess individual contributions.

Treats contributions routed through conduits and intermediaries as coming from both the original giver and the conduit, and requires conduits to report the original source and intended recipient, closing a route for disguised giving.

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees and their corporate and union sponsors, wealthy donors who give through conduits, and broadcasters. PACs would have faced a hard aggregate cap, conduits would have faced new reporting duties, and TV and radio stations would have had to sell airtime to capped candidates at a 30% discount, while the bill also replaces the current 'lowest unit charge' standard for candidate ads with a 'normal and usual unit charge' set by regulators.

drawbacks.text: The $500,000 spending cap is voluntary, so only candidates who opt in are bound by it; a candidate who refuses the cap faces no spending limit at all, and an opponent who outspends a capped candidate is not automatically checked.
The tax credit is nonrefundable, so it helps only people who owe federal income tax, and it flows only to those with $200 or so of spare cash to contribute; it does little for the poorest voters.

The bill swaps the existing 'lowest unit charge' requirement for candidate ads with a 'normal and usual unit charge' as determined by regulators, which could have allowed stations to charge non-capped candidates more than current law requires.
A candidate who sticks to the $500,000 cap while outside groups spend freely against them gains only disclosure of that spending within 24 hours, not relief from it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks real problems in House elections, including PAC dependence, laundered contributions, and late-breaking untraceable ad spending, and its small-donor credit plus discounted airtime would have made a modest-spending campaign viable. But its main lever, the spending cap, is voluntary and unenforceable against opponents who decline it, the tax credit skews toward taxpayers with some disposable income, and the broadcast-rate rewrite carried a risk of raising rates for candidates who did not opt in. A well-designed bill would have made the incentives firmer and the cap less one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three committees on the day it was introduced, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Roy Dyson introduced the bill on March 15, 1990, with no cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to three committees: House Administration, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce, because it touched election law, the tax code, and broadcast regulation.
In the following weeks it was referred to the Subcommittee on Elections and the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and Finance, and no further action of any kind is recorded.
The bill had zero cosponsors and never reached the House floor; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs, conduit givers, and broadcasters kept the existing rules, and no House candidate faced tighter money limits or independent-expenditure disclosure. Incumbents of both parties were spared a change to the funding environment they run in.

for.name: Rep. Roy Dyson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on March 15, 1990.

against.name: House Administration Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over election law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to its Elections Subcommittee, and took no further action; the bill never received a markup or a floor vote.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax credit provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action on the tax credit proposal.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action on the broadcast rate proposal.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the sponsor attracted zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of the bill never had a chance to show itself.

industries.note: PACs would have been capped at $5,000 in total giving to any House candidate and conduit arrangements would have faced new reporting duties. Their money is a major channel through which organized interests reach House members.

Stations would have had to sell airtime to candidates who accepted the spending cap at 70% of the normal rate, cutting campaign ad revenue. The bill also replaces the existing lowest-unit-charge rule with a 'normal and usual unit charge,' which could have softened the current rate floor.

industries.industry: Wealthy individual donors and contribution conduits
industries.note: In-district individuals would have been capped at $3,000 per candidate and conduits would have had to disclose the original source of every routed contribution, raising the cost of moving large sums anonymously.
